attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: variable set up, game set up, on A button pressed, on B button pressed, on menu button pressed.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new variable and assign it to be randomly selected from a range of values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is setting, or declaring, a variable in JavaScript similar and different to doing so in blocks?

❓ What does the assignment operator = do in this line of code? How does it work?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between the [set variable to] block in the blocks editor, and using the let keyword in JavaScript. Both actions assign an initial value to the variable and allow the variable to be referenced later in the program.

💡 In JavaScript, a single equal sign = represents an assignment operator. This symbol assigns the variable named on the left to a value on the right of the operator.
steps.instructions:
Start the game with a random amount of money for the player to spend!

 

Underneath // variable set up type the word let


In JavaScript, variables are set, or declared, using the keyword let, which appears in blue as a way to indicate that a new variable is being defined.

 

Type the variable name cash, a space, then type =


﻿In JavaScript, a single equal sign (=) is called an assignment operator because it assigns a value to a variable.

 

Add another space, then type randint(5, 15) to assign the variable cash an initial random value, so that the code reads:


let cash = randint(5, 15)

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a candy sprite inside the controller.A event, then set the sprite’s x and y-coordinates to be randomly selected from a range of values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the candy sprite’s code be placed the inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event?

❓ What keyword is used to create a new sprite in JavaScript?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the curly brackets { } used in the controller.A code act as the container that holds the rest of the code inside of it. Point out to the ninja that the block statement inside the curly brackets is indented. Show the ninja how they can press the Tab key to indent the code, if needed.

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between creating a new sprite and declaring a new variable: both use the keyword let. This allows an initial value to be assigned to the variable or sprite, which can be referenced later in the program.
steps.instructions:
Code candy sprites to appear in random positions when the user presses the A button.

 

Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on A button pressed. Use the default property A and default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed.

 

Create a new sprite by opening Sprites, then dragging [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event.


Name the sprite candy, click the palette to open the paint editor, then click My Assets at the top of the screen to select the candy image.

 

Set the candy sprite’s x and y values so that it will appear in a random position on screen. Type candy.x, then use an assignment operator (=) and randint to place the sprite somewhere between 0 and the screen.width. On a blank line below, set candy.y to a random position between 0 and the screen.height.

 

Click ▶ and press the A button to see candy sprites appear in random positions on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type cash, a subtraction assignment operator -=, and the cost of the candy so the cash variable is set to a new value each time the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the value of cash when the A button is pressed?

❓ What does a subtraction and equal sign -= represent? How does it work?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja connect the subtraction assignment operator -= in JavaScript with the [change variable by] block in the blocks editor. Both actions cause the variable to change by a certain value. In this case, the value to the right of the -= ($0.50) is subtracted from the value of cash, each time the A button is pressed.

💡 Remind the ninja that when they are referring to monetary amounts, values should be written in decimals.
steps.instructions:
Let the player know how much the candy costs, and subtract that amount from the cash variable.

 

Open Sprites, then drag [(this) say (:))] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event underneath the code that sets the candy sprite’s position. Update the sprite’s name, then replace the text parameter with a string that tells the user the cost of the candy, such as ”$0.50”

 

On a new line below the sayText code, type cash to access the variable. Add a space, then type a minus sign and an equals sign: -= followed by the cost of the candy 0.50


﻿Together, these symbols create a subtraction assignment operator. They will subtract the value on the right from the variable, then set the variable to the updated value.

 

Click ▶ and press the A button to see each candy sprite appear and say the amount that is being subtracted from the player’s cash.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V ) the code from // on A button pressed into // on B button pressed and update the sprite’s name, image and amount subtracted?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What amount might be subtracted from cash each time the B button is pressed?

❓ What value should be shown in the sayText code?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they should select a reasonable value that matches the pizza sprite. Point out that the initial value of cash will fall in the random range they selected, and as such, the change in value should be less than the maximum value of this range.
steps.instructions:
Add a pizza sprite for the player to spend money on.


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on B button pressed. Change the property to B and use the default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed.


Open Sprites, then drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.B event. Name the sprite pizza and update its image.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the code that sets the candy sprite’s position, says its cost, and updates the cash variable from the controller.A event. Paste (Ctrl + V) the code inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.B event. Then, use the new sprite name in the x, y, and sayText code. Change the amount that is subtracted from cash to a higher number, such as 1.50. Be sure to also update the string in the sayText code, too.


Click ▶ then press the A and B buttons to see both food sprites appear.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check the syntax to make sure each pair of curly brackets has an opening and closing set?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What conditions might be checked when the Menu button is pressed?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The if/else if/else if conditional acts as a block statement nested inside the curly brackets of the controller.menu event. It is indented and contains its own set of curly brackets { } to place code inside of.

💡 Remind the ninja that when a single parenthesis or curly bracket is typed, the editor will automatically add the matching symbol.
steps.instructions:
Code the Menu button to check the current value of the cash variable.

 

Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on menu button. Change the property to menu, and leave the default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed

 

By default, pressing the Menu button in MakeCode will open a menu where users can change settings. Through code, it is possible to customize the Menu button, just like the A and B buttons.


Open Logic and drag [if/else] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.menu event. Click to the right of the keyword else, type if () , then {}

 

With the cursor inside the new pair of curly brackets, press Enter to add a blank line below. After the closing curly bracket, type a second else if () so that the code looks like: } else if () {

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the true inside the parentheses of the if condition with an equality operator that checks the value of the cash variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does a double equal sign == represent in JavaScript? How does it work?

❓ What will happen if the value of cash is equal to 0, when the Menu button is pressed?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In JavaScript, a double equal sign == represents an equality operator. This symbol checks to see if the value on the left of the operator is equal to the value on the right. If the value of cash is equal to 0 when the Menu button is pressed, then the if condition’s code will run.

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between the equality operator and the comparison blocks in the blocks editor. Both actions are able to check for equal values on either side of the symbol.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Create a win condition for the user.

 

The goal of the game is for the user to spend exactly as much money as they have. So, if the value of the cash variable is 0 when the user presses the Menu button, they win.

 

Replace true inside the parentheses of the if condition with cash == 0. The double equal sign (==) is called an equality operator.


Unlike the assignment operator, which assigns a value to a variable, the equality operator checks the value. If the values on each side of the equality operator == are the same, the statement is true, and the code in the if condition will run.

 

Inside the curly brackets of the if condition, add a game.splash screen telling the player they won by spending all of their money followed by game.gameOver(true).

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use quotation marks to separate the strings from the cash variable in game.splash?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should quotation marks be placed in the code? Where should + and the variable’s name be placed?

❓ How will the project know how much cash is left?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the process of joining, or concatenating, strings and variables. Point out to the ninja that the string must be contained by quotation marks, a plus sign + must be used to join the two values, then the variable’s name should be listed. Encourage the ninja to double check their work to make sure they’ve included the correct symbols and spacing.
steps.instructions:
Encourage the player to keep spending if they have money left.

 

Update the first else if condition to check if the value of cash is greater than 0. Replace true by typing cash > 0 . The greater-than sign (>) is a relational operator.

 

Inside the curly brackets of this else if condition, add a game.splash screen with a string that tells the player they still have money left to spend, like: “Cash left: $”

 

After the string, type a plus sign (+) then cash


﻿This will concatenate, or join, the string and the variable so that a sentence is displayed that includes the value of the cash variable.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a plus sign (+) to concatenate, or join, the string and and the variable so that a sentence is displayed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should quotation marks be placed? Where should the + and variable’s name be placed?

❓ How will the project know how much cash was overspent?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the process of joining, or concatenating, strings and variables. Point out to the ninja that the string must be contained by quotation marks, a plus sign + must be used to join the two values, then the variable’s name should be listed. Encourage the ninja to double check their work to make sure they’ve included the correct symbols and spacing.

💡 Point out to the ninja the logic of the variable’s value. Each time a new food sprite is added, its designated price is subtracted from the current value of cash. If the variable’s value is less than 0 when the Menu button is pressed, the program will report a negative number. In order for it to show as a positive number, a minus sign - should be placed in front of cash.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Create a lose condition if the player spends too much money.

 

Update the second else if condition to check if the value of cash is less than 0. Replace true by typing cash < 0. The less-than sign (<) is another relational operator.

 

Inside the curly brackets, add a game.splash screen with a string that tells the player they spent too much money, like: “You overspent by: $”

 

After the string, type a plus sign (+) then cash


This will concatenate, or join, the string and the variable so that a sentence is displayed that includes the value of the cash variable. Because the value of cash will be less than 0, use a minus sign (-) before the variable name to show the value as a positive number, like: -cash

 

Then add game.gameOver(false) to end the game.

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help users understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? How might you use the value of cash in the dialog boxes?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!

 

Open Scene, drag [set background color to (color)] into the editor underneath // game set up. Click between the parentheses to set a color parameter using a number 1-15.

 

Open Game and drag [splash (title)] onto a blank line underneath the background color code to give the player instructions. Update the string parameters using concatenation, so that the splash screens share directions for the user to follow, including telling them how much money they have to spend.

 

Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Shop ‘Til You Drop
subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses assignment, equality, and relational operators to track money spent and calculate how much remains.

validationItems.text: Declare a cash variable and assign it a random value.
Use A, B, and menu controller button pressed events.
Create candy and pizza sprites and set their positions randomly. Make each sprite say a string, telling their cost.
After a sprite is spawned, use the subtraction assignment operator to update the value of the cash variable.
Use an if and two else if statements that check when cash is equal to 0, less than 0, and greater than 0
Use three splash functions that share a message based on the value of cash. Use concatenation to display the value of cash in two of the splash functions.
Use the gameOver function to end the game based on the value of cash.
Add a background color and instructions using the splash function.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about assignment and equality operators, which can be used to assign, change, and check for a variable’s value. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: One Equals Sign or Two?
badges.description: Use the correct symbols to create assignment and equality operators to assign, change, and check for a variable’s value in JavaScript.

badges.title: Let There Be Variables
badges.description: Create a variable using let in JavaScript.

badges.title: Concatenation Station
badges.description: Concatenate two or more strings together using the + operator.

badges.title: Asset Depreciation
badges.description: Use the subtraction assignment operator to decrease the value of a number variable.

badges.title: Incremental Growth
badges.description: Use the addition assignment operator to increase the value of a number variable.

badges.title: I’m Thinking of a Number
badges.description: Use the askForNumber function to assign a user-inputted value to a variable.

badges.title: It’s Back on the Menu
badges.description: Write code that runs when the Menu button is pressed.
